content: Steatorrhea refers to the presence of non-solid stools that are characterized by an excessive fat content due to malabsorption. These stools may float, appear oily, and emit a foul odor. Patients may experience oily anal leakage or varying degrees of fecal incontinence. The condition is marked by increased fat excretion, which can be quantified by measuring fecal fat levels. Although there is no universally accepted definition, fat excretion exceeding 0.3 grams per kilogram per day is generally considered diagnostic of steatorrhea. Steatorrhea can be classified into three types based on its underlying cause: intestinal, biliary, and pancreatic. It arises from either structural abnormalities in the digestive tract or defects in the synthesis or secretion of enzymes necessary for fat metabolism. Common causes include celiac disease, choledocholithiasis, cystic fibrosis, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, hypolipidemic drugs, inflammatory bowel disease, and small bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome. Risk factors for developing steatorrhea include these same conditions, as well as the use of certain medications. If left untreated, steatorrhea can result in severe malnutrition due to the gastrointestinal tract's inability to absorb fat-soluble vitamins, leading to significant weight loss. Complications may include anemia, intestinal obstruction, and further weight loss. However, with appropriate treatment, the prognosis is generally favorable. The gold standard for diagnosing steatorrhea is the 72-hour fecal fat determination test. Mild cases of steatorrhea may present with frothy, foul-smelling stools that are greasy in appearance and difficult to flush. Patients may also experience abdominal pain, bloating, and heartburn. Severe cases can lead to malnutrition, dehydration, anemia, muscle weakness, weight loss, skin issues, neurological problems, and osteoporosis. On physical examination, patients often appear emaciated due to the loss of subcutaneous fat. Other notable findings may include a distended abdomen, orthostatic hypotension, ecchymoses, and signs of hypocalcemia such as Chvostek and Trousseau signs. Laboratory tests, including quantitative stool fat analysis, can aid in diagnosis. Techniques such as acid steatocrit, near-infrared reflectance analysis (NIRA), and Sudan III staining may also be utilized. Imaging studies, including X-rays, CT scans, and MRIs, do not typically reveal findings specific to steatorrhea but may help identify underlying causes. Management of steatorrhea involves addressing the underlying cause, controlling diarrhea, and correcting nutritional deficiencies. Surgical intervention is generally reserved for refractory cases or pre-malignant complications, such as Enteropathy-Associated T-cell Lymphoma (EATL) or ulcerative jejunitis (UJ). In cases of EATL, surgery may be necessary to address ulcerative or stenotic lesions and to prevent bowel perforation during subsequent chemotherapy. Post-surgical treatment may include immunotherapy, chemotherapy, and/or stem cell transplantation. Primary prevention strategies include smoking cessation, alcohol avoidance, minimizing the use of medications that disrupt normal bowel flora (e.g., certain antibiotics), and consuming a diet rich in dietary fiber.
